title: I'm Klook's CEO. I train for Hyrox and read complaint emails for fun.
excerpt: Klook's CEO, Ethan Lin, works out twice a day, carves out time for personal projects, and reads customer complaints emails for research — and fun.
content_html:
I'm the CEO of Klook. I spend my free time scrolling through customer complaint emails — and Hyrox training.

As told to Aditi Bharade

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-17T01:00:02.263Z

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Ethan Lin, the 40-year-old cofounder and CEO of travel platform Klook, who is based in Hong Kong. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences.

I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices.

As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days.

An 8 a.m. dopamine boost

Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee.

Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up.

I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support.

After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic.

I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off

I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game.

I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week.

Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day.

When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me.

I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me.

Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day.

I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them

I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed.

The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?"

It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive.

I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples.

I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m.

Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed.

As a CEO, my time is very fragmented: I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing.

Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information.

My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m.

After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run. That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper.

The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective.

I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m.

In 2014, I left a stable banking job to cofound Klook, a platform where people can book travel experiences.

I was 27, had no experience in tech or product, and bootstrapped the business with the savings my cofounders and I had built up. Now, the company is almost 2,000 employees-strong across 25 offices.

As a 40-year-old CEO, I spend most of my time on work and fitness. Here's how I bring my A-game on busy work days.

An 8 a.m. dopamine boost

Fitness is really important to me. It's a dopamine boost in the morning; it works better than coffee.

Each week, I go to the gym five to six times, mostly in the morning before work, around 7 or 8 a.m. That helps me wake up.

I have a light meal, and then I hit the gym for some strength training. I participated in Hyrox in Bangkok a few weeks ago. Klook is Hyrox's travel partner across Asia, and I like to show support.

After my morning workout, I have a light meal that helps me start the day feeling very energetic.

I reach the office around 9 a.m., then AI automations help me kick off

I have several AI projects in the works that help me keep on top of my game.

I have an AI automation set up that sends me a weekly Monday morning summary email, giving me a quick refresh on what's happening each week.

Other AI automations work like think tanks for me, acting like a consultant, industry expert, communication strategist, analyst, and so on, brainstorming with me. One thing I enjoy about AI is that it feels like you're working with many experts every day.

When it comes to drafting emails, I feed AI the skeletons of the content and structure and let it write a draft for me because English isn't my first language, but the critical thinking and judgment have to come from me.

I need to remind myself to be mindful because they all sound right, and I need to be the one deciding what information is really suitable for me.

Before AI, when you worked on a project or task or sent emails, you would get a few hours or days of break before you got a response, or the next piece of information. Right now, that part is pretty much instant, so we end up basically working nonstop. I feel like I'm being mentally challenged more and more every day.

I scroll through customer complaint emails — and enjoy reading them

I'm copied on all Klook customer inquiry or complaint email chains, and I enjoy reading them every day as they come in. In the last 12 years, that's one habit I haven't changed.

The emails often look like: "I booked a day for this activity, but can I change to another day? The system doesn't support it," or "I wrote my name wrong. Can I get entry into this venue without the right name? Can you change it?"

It's something AI can help summarize, but I like to get them randomly every day, even on weekends, because you cannot predict when a customer will submit a complaint. It's like TikTok — swipe, swipe, you never know what's coming next. It's quite addictive.

I don't respond directly to them — that would be a bit awkward — but scrolling through complaints gives me enough frequent data points and real case studies to get a sense of our customers' problems. When we actually conduct analyses or prioritize which problems to solve, I have enough tangible examples.

I'm in the office until at least 7 p.m.

Most days, I'm in the office until 7 to 8 p.m., although other days can get quite late. That's also why I try to protect my morning workouts to kick-start the day, as my evening workouts aren't guaranteed.

As a CEO, my time is very fragmented: I spend half an hour on one task, 15 minutes on another, and an hour on something else. I get sucked into a lot of projects and meetings but often don't have time to sit and think about how they're linked to see if anything's missing.

Every week, I block off two to three hours from my calendar for personal reflection. I'll use that to finish a project or task, or consolidate information.

My second workout, followed by bed at 1 a.m.

After work, about twice a week at night, I hit cardio. I do a light zone-two run. That means a four- to eight-kilometer run at a not-too-crazy pace, depending on how busy my day has been. This helps me build endurance and sleep better, although I'm already a pretty deep sleeper.

The last hour or so of my day is my quiet time. This involves some email clean-up, prepping for the next day, and reading things outside technology and travel to give myself a different perspective.

I'm normally asleep by 1 a.m.
